cells.tense: You're here, with your hands on it.
cells.verb: keeping two things alive at once and tending both so they keep growing
cells.place: in the part of you that stays pointed at where you're going
cells.ask: Let one person see what you've been giving to keep this moving — and let one thing that's finished be finished. What comes back is the growing without the gripping: care that doesn't wear you down.
cells.core:
You're here, with your hands on it. You're moving toward something and you're not burning the ground you move over — the things that need tending get tended, the two demands that both want you both get fed, and you still know which way you're walking. It isn't force. It's upkeep, done on the way.

That kind of tending is mostly invisible, and it doesn't have to stay that way. Let one person see what it's cost you to keep this moving. And let one thing you've carried to completion actually be complete — set down, not dropped. What returns is the same motion with less grip in it: growth that doesn't exhaust the grower.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving and tending at the same time, and neither is starving the other.

cells.tense: You're already living in a future where it all has to be kept alive.
cells.verb: tending every inch of the ground so hard nothing has room to grow on its own
cells.place: in the part of you that stays pointed at where you're going
cells.ask: Picture it already arrived — and let yourself feel what it's like when it has. Stay in that for a minute before you touch anything else. What comes back is care that doesn't wear you down, growing without the gripping.
cells.core:
You're already living in a future where it all has to be kept alive. Every resource counted, every pace adjusted, both demands watched so closely they can't breathe — and the forward motion you had is going into upkeep instead of distance. You're tending so hard the growing has become your job rather than its own.

The way back is not to tend less. It's to feel, for once, what the tending was for. Picture the thing arrived. Let yourself have what it would be like to stand there, done — not as a plan, as a feeling. Stay in it before you touch anything else. What returns is the same care without the clutch in it: growth that happens because you made room, not because you held on.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it alive so carefully it can't grow.

cells.tense: You've stopped tending a thing you're still walking toward.
cells.verb: letting what grows go dry while the motion carries on without it
cells.place: in the part of you that stays pointed at where you're going
cells.ask: Say out loud what you still want from this — not the plan, the wanting — and let that do the pulling. What comes back is the tending, without having to force it: care that doesn't wear you down.
cells.core:
You've stopped tending a thing you're still walking toward. The direction is there — you haven't turned around — but somewhere back there the upkeep got dropped, and you're moving past things that needed watering without stopping. Both demands still exist. Neither is getting fed. The motion is running on what's already stored.

Don't try to shove effort back into the tending. Go to the hope instead. Say out loud what you still want from this — not the task list, the wanting underneath it, the one that's survived everything so far. Energy there is what pulls the tending back along with it. What returns is care that comes because you still want the thing, not because you made yourself, and that kind of care doesn't exhaust.
cells.sheetLine: You're still moving toward it. You just stopped looking after it.

cells.tense: You're already doing the tending, and you call it nothing.
cells.verb: keeping two things alive at once and letting the credit go to the momentum
cells.place: in the part of you that stays pointed at where you're going
cells.ask: Tell one person plainly what it's cost you to keep both of these going. What comes back is tending you can feel yourself doing: care that doesn't wear you down, because you know it's yours.
cells.core:
You're already doing the tending, and you call it nothing. Two things are both alive because you've been feeding both; the motion keeps its direction because you keep clearing the way. And when anyone asks, you say it's just moving along, as if the ground were watering itself. The care is running. The name on it is blank.

The simplest version of the fix is the whole fix. Tell one person, plainly, what it's cost you to keep both of these going — not for sympathy, just so it's been said in a room. Once the giving is visible, you can see yourself giving it, and tending you can see is tending you can rest from. What returns is care you don't have to keep secret from yourself, and that's the kind that doesn't exhaust.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping this alive. You just haven't said it's you.
